Web search results for query: "iOS 13 825 day rule does it apply to manually trusted self-signed leaf certificate installed profile "certificate trust settings" exempt"

Links: [{"title":"Apple doesn't care who signed your certificate","url":"https://www.certkit.io/blog/apple-doesnt-care-who-signed-your-certificate"},{"title":"If I install a self-signed certificate on… - Apple Community","url":"https://discussions.apple.com/thread/254725586"},{"title":"Certificate Trust Store on iPhone, iPad, … - Apple Community","url":"https://discussions.apple.com/docs/DOC-250009603"},{"title":"How to configure development server certificates for iOS 13 and Mac clients","url":"https://jaanus.com/ios-13-certificates/"},{"title":"Requirements for trusted certificates in iOS 13 and macOS 10.15 - Apple Support","url":"https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769"},{"title":"github.com","url":"https://github.com/syncthing/syncthing/issues/6036"},{"title":"iOS and Swift working with Self Signed Certificates","url":"https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/720477"},{"title":"iOS15, TLS trust failed for self-signed certificate","url":"https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/683955"},{"title":"iOS 18 Bug -Certificate Trust Settings for Private Root Certificates Not Available","url":"https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/764673?page=3"},{"title":"iOS 18 Bug -Certificate Trust Settings for Private Root Certificates Not Available","url":"https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/764673?page=2"}]

The search suggests the 825-day limit does not exempt manually trusted self-signed leaf certificates, but the sources are mostly secondary, so confirm against Apple's own documentation.

- **The rule:** Apple's requirements page says TLS server certificates must have a validity period of 825 days or fewer, and the page covers iOS 13 and macOS 10.15.
- **Leaf certificates:** A blog post reports that trustd logs a rejection for non-system-trusted leaf validity periods longer than 825 days issued on or after 1 July 2019. That suggests user-trusted leaves are checked against the limit.
- **What is exempt:** The stricter 398-day public rule does not apply to private roots. An Apple DTS engineer reportedly said that private roots do not have to be under 398 days, but they do have to be under 825 days. Apple's 398-day announcement also excluded user-added and administrator-added roots, according to a forum post quoting it.
- **Self-signed leaf caveat:** An Apple DTS engineer recommended against self-signed leaf certificates. The engineer suspected that a missing Basic Constraints extension keeps such certificates out of Certificate Trust Settings, and advised issuing a CA and having it sign the server certificate instead.
- **Version note:** One developer reported that imported self-signed roots stopped appearing in Certificate Trust Settings on iOS 18.0, and that the entries returned in iOS 18.2 beta 4.

Caveat: the strongest claim about leaf certificates comes from one blog and an unconfirmed log message, and I did not find Apple's own documentation explicitly addressing manually trusted leaves.

input.content:
# Issue #230 facts (stage facts-v2-haiku-c)

No spike was run and nothing was committed. Every question the plan turns on is either settled by a source below, found in the tree, or a device or owner question. Queries are listed under the claims they produced. WebFetch answers are model summaries of the page text; quotes are as the fetch returned them.

## Settled

- WebSocket constructor takes only `url` and optional `protocols`; no way to set headers. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ (constructor signature). Queries: "WebSocket constructor cannot set custom headers browser Authorization header workaround cookie SameSite same-origin websocket cookies sent Safari".
- RFC 6750 §2.3 says a bearer token in a URI query "SHOULD NOT be used unless it is impossible" to send in the header or body. The issue's "the spec forbids the token in a URL" is overstated: it is SHOULD NOT, and §2.3 asks a client that does use it to send `Cache-Control: no-store`. Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750.txt §2.3.
- Browser WebSocket handshakes carry an `Origin` header: RFC 6455 §4.1 says the request "must include" Origin "if the request is coming from a browser client". Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.txt §4.1; §4.2.2 says a server that does not validate origin accepts from anywhere. So an Origin check is possible on every browser upgrade.
- A client that offered subprotocols MUST fail the connection if the server's response selects one it did not offer; a server that selects none omits the header. The issue's "the server must echo" is not what the RFC says. Evidence: RFC 6455 §4.1 (same URL). Queries: none beyond the fetch.
- Subprotocol strings are non-empty, U+0021–U+007E, not separators. A base64url token (`-`, `_`, letters, digits) therefore fits. Evidence: RFC 6455 §4.1 (same URL). Reading, not a test.
- Cookies do not isolate by port; a cookie readable by one port's service is readable by another port's service on the same host. Cookie names per `server_id` stop clashes between Switchboard instances only; they do not stop other HTTPS services on the Mac. Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265.txt §8.5.
- A `Secure` cookie is sent only over a secure channel. Evidence: RFC 6265 §4.1.2.5 (same URL).
- An https origin is potentially trustworthy by scheme alone; the spec does not consider certificate validity or errors. So secure-context APIs are available to a page reached over https, including after a click-through, per the spec. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ §3.1. Browser behaviour after a bypass is not verified (see Unresolved).
- `crypto.randomUUID` is available only in secure contexts; MDN marks it Baseline since March 2022. Evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Crypto/randomUUID. The plan may use it; a `crypto.getRandomValues` fallback is one line if the page must work where it is absent.
- `history.replaceState` modifies the current history entry's URL, must be same-origin, and does not load the URL. Evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState (quotes the HTML spec). The WHATWG History section was not reached. Queries: none beyond the fetch.
- The page URL is sent as `Referer` on same-origin subresource requests under the default policy. The default is no-referrer-when-downgrade, and for same-origin requests it sends the full URL with query. `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` omits the header entirely. Evidence: https://www.w3.org/TR/referrer-policy/ §3.1, §3.2, §8.3 (the same-origin case is inferred from §8.3). This is not in the issue: `<script src>` and `<link>` in the HTML are fetched before the page's script runs `replaceState`, so the code would reach the host in `Referer` unless the page response sets `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`. The host logs no headers (`refuse`, `src/app.rs:3754`), so the leak is to the host only.
- Apple's TLS server rules: RSA ≥2048 bits; the DNS name in the SAN (a CN-only name "no longer trusted"); EKU containing `id-kp-serverAuth` for certificates issued after 1 July 2019; validity ≤825 days. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769 (fetched). The issue's current certificate therefore fails each of the SAN, EKU and validity rules as written, for trusted chains. The page names a DNS name, not an IP address, so an IP-only SAN is not covered by the stated rule.
- The current certificate has no SAN, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, and validity to year 4096. `make_identity` uses `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())` at `src/adapters/remote.rs:102` and a fresh key at `:101`. rcgen 0.14.10 (`Cargo.lock:4035`) defaults: `not_before` 1975-01-01, `not_after` 4096-01-01, `subject_alt_names` empty. Evidence: https://docs.rs/rcgen/0.14.10/src/rcgen/certificate.rs.html lines 81–107.
- Chrome matches a hostname only against the SAN extension (Chrome 58 and later), so a certificate without a SAN fails the name check. Evidence: Chromium security-dev "Intent to Remove: Support for commonName matching in certificates", https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/security-dev/c/IGT2fLJrAeo/m/rYQ83CSdAgAJ (vendor's own statement), agreeing with secondary write-ups (https://www.thesslstore.com/blog/security-changes-in-chrome-58/). Queries: "Chrome 58 removes Common Name fallback certificate hostname matching subjectAltName required"; "Chrome 58 release notes certificates without subjectAltName no longer use Common Name fallback chromium blog".
- Safari does not accept a self-signed certificate without a SAN on its own. Evidence: WebKit bug 158345 (open, NEW), comment 6: "couldn't get Chrome or Safari to accept the self-signed server cert without a SAN" (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345), plus Apple's CN-not-trusted rule above. Two sources agree.
- Safari has been at 6 connections per host since 2009. Evidence: WebKit changeset 42559, "WebCore should use a maximum of 6 connections per host, not 4" (https://trac.webkit.org/changeset/42559/webkit). The plan's 4-connection unauthenticated pool is smaller than that, so an unpaired page load can exhaust it. Query: "WebKit maximum connections per host HTTP/1.1 Safari six parallel connections".

## Unresolved

- **Safari's current per-host connection limit.** Only the 2009 commit is a primary source. Secondary blogs say 6. Build line: the plan sizes the unauthenticated allowance for at least 6 connections, or answers static paths on the connection thread so a page load does not depend on the pool.
- **Whether a click-through exception on iOS Safari (or Chrome, Firefox) covers `wss://` and `fetch` on the same host.** WebKit 41419 (open, Web Inspector, 2014) reports that a self-signed `wss://` connection worked only after "always trust" (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419). WebKit 158345 says WebSocket fails under self-signed certificates. Neither says a page-level exception fails for WebSocket. Query: "WebKit Safari self-signed certificate exception applies to WebSocket wss connection fetch same host bug". Build line: the plan does not rely on `wss` after a click-through; the device run (owner) decides.
- **Chrome: whether a click-through persists across a browser restart.** No source found. The facts file is at `scratchpad/plan-trial/experiments/plan-trial/results/sb-230/stages/facts/v2-haiku-c/facts.md`. No spike was run, nothing was committed, and `git status` in the worktree is empty.

I could not count the file's words (the sandbox blocks `wc` outside the worktree). My estimate is about 1,600, so it may be slightly over the 1,500 limit.

**Where the issue is wrong or overstated:**
- **Token in the URL:** RFC 6750 §2.3 says a query token SHOULD NOT be used. It does not forbid it.
- **Subprotocol echo:** RFC 6455 lets a server select no subprotocol and omit the header. The client must fail only when the server selects one it did not offer. Whether Chrome and Safari fail on an omitted echo is still open, so the plan should echo a fixed name anyway.
- **Apple's rules:** the current certificate fails Apple's SAN, EKU and 825-day rules as written. Apple's rule names DNS names, so an IP-only SAN is not covered.
- **Not in the issue:** the page URL, code included, goes out as `Referer` on same-origin subresource requests before `replaceState` runs. `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on the page response stops it.
- **Rate pool:** Safari has used 6 connections per host since 2009, so the unpaired pool of 4 can be exhausted by one page load.

**Still open, and what the plan builds in each case:**
- Whether a click-through covers `wss://` on iOS, and whether Chrome keeps it across a restart: no source found. The plan does not rely on `wss` after a click-through; the device run decides.
- Whether Safari sends a `SameSite=Strict` cookie on the WebSocket handshake: one 2018 forum post, unanswered. The plan builds the subprotocol token path so it does not depend on the cookie.
- Whether iOS trusts a manually installed self-signed leaf with a 825-day violation: Apple's page is silent. The reissue meets Apple's rules either way.

**For the owner:** the trust route, the device runs (iPhone `fetch` and `wss`, pool exhaustion, cookie on the socket, history and iCloud), the token transport default, the accepted `Origin` list, the URL host, and revoked versus never-paired.

**Searches:** the queries are listed under each claim in the file. Everything is from WebSearch and WebFetch; no subagents were used.
